lead: The second most important art gallery in Spain, in a 17th-century Baroque palace. From Valencian Gothic to Sorolla, via Velázquez, Goya, El Greco, Botticelli and Van Dyck.

The Museo de Bellas Artes de Valencia — popularly known as the Museo de San Pío V — occupies the former Colegio Seminario founded in 1683 on the banks of the Turia Garden, between the Real and Trinidad bridges. Its origins are tied to the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Carlos, founded in 1768, and to the 19th-century confiscations of Church property, which fed its collections with works from suppressed convents. After several changes of location, the collections were finally installed in the Baroque San Pío V building in 1946.

It is the second most important art gallery in Spain and the visit is completely free. Its collection runs through the history of Valencian, Spanish and European art from the 14th to the 19th century with works of the very highest rank.

items.kicker: 14th–15th centuries · One of the most important collections in Spain
items.title: Valencian Primitives · Gothic Painting
items.subtitle: Gonçal Peris Sarrià · Starnina · Altarpiece of Fray Bonifacio Ferrer
items.body: The collection of Valencian primitives is the museum’s jewel and one of the most important groups of Gothic painting in Spain. It reflects the international school of painting that flourished in Valencia during the 15th century, when the city was a great commercial and cultural centre of the Mediterranean. The masterpieces of Gonçal Peris Sarrià represent the highlight of this period. The Altarpiece of Fray Bonifacio Ferrer, commissioned from the Florentine artist Gherardo Starnina, is also preserved, one of the museum’s most valuable pieces for its exceptional detail.
facts: Altarpiece of Fray Bonifacio Ferrer · Starnina · Extraordinary Florentine detail

items.kicker: 16th century · Valencia as the gateway of the Renaissance in Spain
items.title: Renaissance and Mannerism
items.subtitle: Joan de Joanes · Il Pinturicchio · Hieronymus Bosch · Botticelli
items.body: In the 16th century, Valencia was an important commercial centre and the main gateway of the Italian Renaissance into Spain. This room includes the only Botticelli portrait displayed in Spain, as well as works by Il Pinturicchio — a collaborator of Raphael in the Sistine Chapel —, Hieronymus Bosch and Joan de Joanes, the most influential Valencian painter of the 16th century. Andrea del Sarto and works by the Mannerist Luis de Morales are also preserved. The collection reflects the cultural exchanges between Valencia, Italy and the Low Countries.
facts: Botticelli portrait · The only one displayed in Spain · Renaissance Room

items.kicker: 17th century · Velázquez · El Greco · Ribera · Murillo · Van Dyck
items.title: Spanish and European Baroque · The Golden Age
items.subtitle: Velázquez Self-Portrait · José de Ribera · El Greco · Flemish school
items.body: The Baroque room is the most international in the museum. Standing out are the Self-Portrait of Diego Velázquez — one of only two known, the other being in Las Meninas — and Saint John the Baptist by El Greco. By José de Ribera, the spectacular Saint Sebastian Attended by Saint Irene and Her Maid is preserved. The Flemish collection includes Van Dyck with Don Francisco de Moncada, an artist with very little presence in Spanish museums. Italian Baroque painting is represented by Luca Giordano, Giovanni Baglione and Matthias Stom.
facts: Velázquez Self-Portrait · He only painted himself here and in Las Meninas

items.kicker: Late 18th century · Goya and his contemporaries
items.title: Francisco de Goya and Neoclassicism
items.subtitle: Portrait of Joaquina Candado · Vicente López · Academia de San Carlos
items.body: The museum preserves a notable group of works by Francisco de Goya, among which the Portrait of doña Joaquina Candado stands out. The first floor of the old building houses the paintings related to the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Carlos — founded in 1768 — with sketches by Ignacio Vergara and early works by Vicente López, one of the great portraitists of the transition between the 18th and 19th centuries. The “Valencian school of flowers” with works by Benito Espinos completes this period.
facts: Portrait of doña Joaquina Candado · Goya · One of the best works of the period

items.kicker: 7 rooms devoted to Sorolla · The jewel in the crown
items.title: Sorolla and 19th-Century Valencian Painting
items.subtitle: Joaquín Sorolla · Ignacio Pinazo · José Benlliure · Muñoz Degrain
items.body: The Museo de Bellas Artes de Valencia preserves the most complete Sorolla collection outside the Museo Sorolla in Madrid: seven rooms spread over two floors cover his whole career. The Grupa Valenciana, which portrays his children at a country party, is one of the best-loved works. Ignacio Pinazo, founder of the luminous Valencian school of the 19th century, and José Benlliure, with his intimist sensibility, complete the great chapter of 19th-century Valencian painting. The collection of 19th-century Spanish landscape painters also stands out.
facts: Grupa Valenciana · Sorolla · Portrays his children at a Valencian country party

items.kicker: Baroque architecture · 17th–18th century · Juan Bautista Pérez Castiel
items.title: The Building · Cloister and Embajador Vich Courtyard
items.subtitle: Former San Pío V Seminary College · Triple-arcade cloister · 1683
items.body: The museum building is a work of art in itself. Built from 1683 as the San Pío V Seminary College on the commission of Archbishop Juan Tomás de Rocabertí, its Baroque architecture was designed by Juan Bautista Pérez Castiel — master builder of Valencia Cathedral. The almost square plan is organised around a cloister of superimposed triple arcades with five arches on each side. Inside the museum is also preserved the Embajador Vich Courtyard, one of the most important Renaissance courtyards of the 16th century, rebuilt here in 2006.
facts: Embajador Vich Courtyard · 16th-century Renaissance courtyard rebuilt in the museum in 2006

blocks.title: Tips for visiting the museum
items: Admission is free every day — one of the most accessible museums in Spain
If time is limited, prioritise the Velázquez Self-Portrait, the Sorolla room and the Valencian Primitives collection
The Embajador Vich Courtyard is the most beautiful in the museum: a 16th-century Renaissance courtyard rebuilt here in 2006
The museum organises lectures, performing arts and film seasons: check the programme at museobellasartesvalencia.gva.es
It is next to the Turia Garden and the Jardines del Real: combine the visit with a walk in the park
It is closed on Mondays: it is the museum’s only day off, so plan your visit from Tuesday to Sunday
